description: ¡Únete a nuestro equipo en el NASA Space Apps Villavicencio! Somos Martín y un amigo: programadores juniors, estudiantes de colegio, y yo también diseñador. Vamos con el reto CLPS Lunar Mission Browser: plataforma interactiva de misiones lunares de la NASA con datos automáticos y predictor de éxito de aterrizaje.
summary:
Lunar Polar Planner is a web tool that helps mission planners decide where and when to land near the Moon’s south pole. You pick candidate sites, including Artemis III regions, and a date range. The tool shows where the Sun and Earth sit in the sky from each site. It then turns that into plain answers: when solar power is available, when a direct radio link to Earth is possible, and which start dates keep both for a whole mission. A banner says whether a given moment is good or not, and NASA’s south pole animation (SVS 5228) plays in sync with the chosen date.

Near the pole the Sun skims the horizon and Earth hovers at its edge, so a few degrees decide whether a lander has power or contact. Comparing sites by hand is slow. Our tool shows that trade-off in seconds.

Positions come from published astronomical series and agree with NASA/JPL Horizons within 0.03° on 25 dates in 2026. Today it assumes a smooth Moon; real LRO terrain is our next step.
details:
What it does and how it works
Lunar Polar Planner compares landing sites near the Moon’s south pole. The user picks sites (eight Artemis III-style presets or any custom point) and a time window of up to a year. The tool calculates where Earth and the Sun are in the sky from each site, hour by hour. From that it works out when the Sun is above the horizon (solar power), when Earth is above it (direct-to-Earth radio), and which start dates keep both for a mission of a chosen length. The results show as a plain-language banner (“Good moment: power and a link to Earth”), a sky view, a polar map, timelines, a comparison table, and buttons that jump to the best start dates. NASA’s south pole animation (SVS 5228) plays in sync with the selected date.

Benefits and intended impact
Near the pole a few degrees decide whether a lander has power or contact. Our tool lets a student, engineer or mission planner see that trade-off in seconds, without astronomy software. We hope it helps people think about site and date choices for polar missions such as Artemis III.

Tools and technology
A single HTML page with JavaScript and Canvas 2D, no server. Our own engine implements J. Meeus’s lunar, solar and libration series. We validated it against NASA/JPL Horizons (DE441): the Earth and Sun sub-points agree within 0.03° on 25 dates in 2026. We used the NASA SVS 5228 video. We tested in a browser with Playwright. AI assistance (Claude) helped build and test the code and write text; the team should state this in the AI-use field.

Creativity
Instead of tables of angles, the tool answers “is now a good moment?” and “which start dates work?”. Optional controls model a terrain horizon and a mast height. The NASA footage follows the cursor date, and outside its range it shows the closest look-alike moment and labels it as such.

Factors we considered
Accuracy (validated against NASA data), clarity for non-experts, and phone use. We also considered honesty about limits: the Moon is modeled as smooth, site coordinates are approximate, and the video dates were inferred to within about half a day. Real LRO terrain horizons are our next step. This work is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.
